title: CLAT GK - Test 01
notes: Generated with Haiku 5.5, then independently verified question by question by separate Sonnet agents using fresh searches (two-source rule; claims that could not be confirmed were removed or reworded; ambiguous, unchecked or overlapping questions were dropped). Several primary sources were unreachable, so residual risk is listed below. Not reviewed by a human.
residual: Static-GK explanations cite Wikipedia or exam-prep pages in places where a primary text was not reachable.

passages.title: Budget 2026-27, repo rate holds and a strong Q1 GDP print
passages.text:
Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman presented the Union Budget for 2026-27 in Parliament on 1 February 2026, a Sunday. It was her ninth consecutive Budget. She set the fiscal deficit target for 2026-27 at 4.3 per cent of GDP, or about Rs 16.95 lakh crore, slightly below the 4.4 per cent revised estimate for 2025-26, and said she had fulfilled her 2021-22 commitment to bring the deficit below 4.5 per cent of GDP by 2025-26. The Budget raised capital expenditure to about Rs 12.2 lakh crore and projected the Centre's debt at 55.6 per cent of GDP, with the stated aim of moving towards around 50 per cent by March 2031. Total expenditure was estimated at Rs 53.47 lakh crore.

Five days later, on 6 February 2026, the Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee, chaired by Governor Sanjay Malhotra, kept the policy repo rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent with a neutral stance, leaving the standing deposit facility rate at 5.00 per cent and the marginal standing facility rate and Bank Rate at 5.50 per cent. It was the Governor's first policy review after the Budget. The Committee repeated the decision on 5 June 2026, citing elevated crude oil prices amid the West Asia conflict and concerns about the monsoon. At its meeting of 3 to 5 August 2026, the MPC voted unanimously to hold the rate at 5.25 per cent once more and retained the neutral stance. The RBI projected real GDP growth of 6.7 per cent and consumer price inflation of 5.0 per cent for 2026-27. The repo rate had been lowered in several steps during 2025 before the pause began.

The central bank's growth projection was overtaken by official data on 31 August 2026. The National Statistical Office reported that India's real GDP grew 7.8 per cent in April-June 2026, the first quarter of 2026-27, against the RBI's own estimate of 7 per cent for the quarter. Nominal GDP rose 10.3 per cent to Rs 88.27 lakh crore. Gross value added grew 8.2 per cent, led by services, and gross fixed capital formation rose 11.9 per cent. The growth rate was lower than the upwardly revised 8.6 per cent recorded in the fourth quarter of 2025-26. ICRA raised its full-year forecast to 7.1 per cent from 6.7 per cent, though it flagged a poor monsoon and prolonged West Asia tensions as downside risks.

The MPC met again from 5 to 7 October 2026. Ahead of that meeting, most economists in polls expected the Committee to raise the repo rate by 25 basis points, which would be the first increase since February 2023.

questions.q: The Union Budget presented in Parliament each year is constitutionally described as the 'annual financial statement'. Under which Article of the Constitution is it laid before Parliament?
questions.explanation: Article 112(1) requires the President to cause an estimate of receipts and expenditure for each financial year, the annual financial statement, to be laid before both Houses.

questions.q: The National Statistical Office, which released the Q1 2026-27 GDP estimate, functions under which Union Ministry?
options: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
questions.explanation: GDP estimates are released by the NSO under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI).

questions.assertion: Salaries of Supreme Court judges are not subject to a vote by the Lok Sabha when the Budget is passed.
questions.reason: Such expenditure is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
questions.explanation: Salaries of Supreme Court judges, along with debt charges and certain other items, are charged on the Consolidated Fund and are not put to a vote in the Lok Sabha; so R correctly explains A.

statements: I. The Monetary Policy Committee has six members, three of whom are from the Reserve Bank of India including the Governor as ex-officio chairperson.
II. The inflation target for the MPC is set by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank, at 4 per cent with an upper tolerance level of 6 per cent and a lower level of 2 per cent.
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Section 45ZB provides for a six-member MPC with three RBI members and three government-appointed external members, and the target notified under Section 45ZA is 4 per cent with a 2 to 6 per cent band.

statements: I. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act was enacted in 2003.
II. The Act, as amended in 2018, set a target of limiting the Centre's fiscal deficit to 3 per cent of GDP.
III. The 2018 amendment allows deviation from the fiscal deficit target by up to 1 percentage point of GDP under an escape clause.
questions.explanation: The FRBM Act dates from 2003 (Act 39 of 2003) and, as amended, sets a 3 per cent of GDP fiscal deficit target; the escape clause permits a deviation of up to 0.5 percentage points (one-half per cent), not 1, so III is incorrect.

passages.title: FIFA World Cup 2026: Spain crowned champions
passages.text:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup, the first to be hosted jointly by three nations, ran for 39 days from 11 June to 19 July 2026. It was also the first edition expanded to 48 teams, split into 12 groups of four, a structure that guaranteed every team at least three matches, and featured a record 104 matches across 16 host cities, of which 11 were in the United States, three in Mexico and two in Canada. The opening game on 11 June was played at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City, where Mexico beat South Africa 2-0 through goals from Julian Quinones and Raul Jimenez. South Africa finished the match with nine men, and the game produced three red cards in all.

The tournament ended on 19 July at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where Spain defeated defending champion Argentina 1-0 after extra time before a crowd of 80,663. Ferran Torres, who had come on as a substitute, scored the only goal early in the second period of extra time, in the 106th minute. Argentina had been reduced to ten men late in normal time when Enzo Fernandez received a second yellow card, and goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez made 11 saves, a record for a World Cup final, without being able to deny Spain. The victory gave Spain its second world title.

Spain also dominated the individual honours announced after the final. Midfielder Rodri was named winner of the Golden Ball as the best player of the tournament, while goalkeeper Unai Simon took the Golden Glove after Spain conceded just one goal in the whole tournament. Argentina's captain took the Silver Ball and Mbappe, of France, the Bronze Ball. Pau Cubarsi beat his Spain teammate Lamine Yamal to the best young player award, and the Fair Play award went to the Netherlands. The Golden Boot, however, went to France's Kylian Mbappe, who scored 10 goals, the most at a single World Cup since 1970, and finished two clear of the runner-up, who ended on eight goals. England's Jude Bellingham took third place in the scoring list with seven goals.

For Mbappe, the award extended a remarkable run at the sport's biggest event: he became the first player to win the Golden Boot twice, and his tally lifted him to 22 career World Cup goals, a men's all-time record. For Spain, the result capped a tournament in which its defence was breached only once. The tournament's expanded format meant that the eventual champion had to navigate a new round of 32, introduced because the top two sides from every group and the eight best third-placed teams advanced.

questions.q: Spain's win over Argentina in the 2026 final was its second World Cup title. In which year did Spain win its first, beating the Netherlands 1-0 after extra time?
questions.explanation: Spain won its first World Cup on 11 July 2010 at Soccer City, Johannesburg, beating the Netherlands 1-0 after extra time through an Andres Iniesta goal.

questions.q: Argentina entered the 2026 final as defending champion. Which player won the Golden Ball at the 2022 World Cup, and remains the only player to have won that award twice?
questions.explanation: Lionel Messi was awarded the Golden Ball at the 2022 World Cup and is the only player to have received it twice (2014 and 2022). Mbappe won the 2022 Golden Boot instead.

The 2010 final (Spain v Netherlands) was at Soccer City, Johannesburg; the 2022 final (Argentina v France) at Lusail Stadium, Qatar; the 2026 final at MetLife Stadium; and the 2026 opener at the Estadio Azteca.

statements: I. Kylian Mbappe won the Golden Boot at the 2022 World Cup with eight goals.
II. Argentina beat France in the 2022 final in regulation time, 2-1, without the need for extra time.
questions.explanation: Statement I is correct: Mbappe scored eight goals in 2022, including a hat-trick in the final. Statement II is incorrect: the 2022 final finished 3-3 after extra time and Argentina won 4-2 on penalties.

statements: 1. The FIFA World Cup trophy was designed by the Italian sculptor Silvio Gazzaniga.
2. The trophy is made of 18-carat gold.
3. The trophy weighs about 6.175 kg.
4. The trophy is solid gold throughout, with no hollow interior.
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is incorrect: the trophy is made of 18-carat gold but is hollow inside, so it is not solid gold throughout, and it weighs about 6.175 kg.

passages.title: Article 21 Widened: Menstrual Health and Passive Euthanasia
passages.text:
Two rulings delivered by the Supreme Court in the first quarter of 2026 have widened the reach of the right to life in different directions, and Justice J.B. Pardiwala sat on the bench in both.

On 30 January 2026, a bench of Justices Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan decided Dr. Jaya Thakur v. Government of India. The petition, filed in 2022 by social activist Jaya Thakur, had sought free sanitary pads for girls in classes 6 to 12 and separate toilets for girls in schools. The Court held that menstrual health is part of the right to life under Article 21, and that poor menstrual hygiene management is not merely a sanitation problem but a violation of the fundamental rights to equality, dignity and education. It said the absence of gender-segregated toilets and menstrual hygiene facilities is a constitutional barrier to schooling for adolescent girls, engaging Articles 14, 21 and 21A. The bench directed the Union, the states and the Union Territories to ensure that schools, whether government-run, aided or private, provide free sanitary napkins, maintain functional, gender-segregated toilets and arrange for the safe disposal of menstrual waste. Private schools that fail to comply risk derecognition.

On 11 March 2026, a different bench of Justices Pardiwala and K.V. Viswanathan decided Harish Rana v. Union of India. Rana, reported to be about 31 or 32 years old, had been in a persistent vegetative state for over thirteen years after a fall from the fourth floor of his accommodation in 2013 left him with a severe brain injury. His parents had first approached the Delhi High Court, which declined relief on the ground that he was not on mechanical life support and was not terminally ill. They then came to the Supreme Court, which initially gave them liberty to return if further directions were needed. Two medical boards constituted by the Court later concluded that he had no chance of recovery, and the bench reserved its judgment on 15 January 2026.

The Court allowed withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, including clinically assisted nutrition and hydration, which it treated as medical treatment rather than basic nursing care. It applied the "best interest" principle and the guidelines flowing from Common Cause v. Union of India, as modified in 2023. It waived the usual 30-day reconsideration period because all stakeholders agreed, and directed AIIMS, New Delhi, to admit him to its palliative care department. It also asked the Union government to consider comprehensive legislation on passive euthanasia. He was shifted on 14 March to the palliative care unit at the Dr B.R. Ambedkar Institute Rotary Cancer Hospital, AIIMS, where a team led by Dr Seema Mishra supervised the gradual withdrawal of treatment. Rana died on 24 March 2026. Reports describe it as the first such case of passive euthanasia allowed by a court in India.

Taken together, the judgments show the Court continuing to read Article 21 as more than mere animal existence, covering health, bodily autonomy and dignity from the school toilet to the hospital bed.

questions.q: The Jaya Thakur ruling stressed that menstrual hygiene facilities are linked to the education of girls. Which Article of the Constitution expressly permits the State to make special provisions for women and children despite the bar on discrimination?
questions.explanation: Article 15(3) says nothing in Article 15 prevents the State from making any special provision for women and children.

questions.q: Which seven-judge Supreme Court decision, with a leading opinion by Justice Bhagwati, read the words 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 as requiring a procedure that is fair, just and reasonable, and so underpins the wide modern reading of the right to life?
options: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
questions.explanation: Maneka Gandhi (25 January 1978) held procedure under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable, linking Articles 14, 19 and 21 and departing from Gopalan; the lead opinion was by Justice Bhagwati.

questions.assertion: Before Article 21A existed, the Supreme Court in Unni Krishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh had read a right to free education for children up to a certain age into Article 21.
questions.reason: Article 21A was later inserted into the Constitution by the Eighty-sixth Amendment Act, 2002, and the RTE Act 2009 is the law implementing it.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the 2002 insertion of Article 21A and the 2009 RTE Act do not explain why the Court read the right into Article 21 in 1993; that was done through interpretation alongside Directive Principles (Articles 41, 45, 46).

list1: I. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
II. Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh
III. Common Cause v. Union of India (Constitution Bench)
IV. Aruna Shanbaug v. Union of India
questions.explanation: Maneka Gandhi 1978; Unni Krishnan 1993; Aruna Shanbaug 2011; Common Cause 2018 (9 March 2018).

statements: 1. The Common Cause judgment on the right to die with dignity was delivered by a five-judge Constitution Bench.
2. A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras treated the fundamental rights as separate, watertight compartments, an approach the Supreme Court later departed from.
3. In Unni Krishnan, the Supreme Court held that the right to education up to a professional degree flows directly from Article 21.
4. In Aruna Shanbaug v. Union of India, the Supreme Court allowed passive euthanasia in certain circumstances under court monitoring.
questions.explanation: Only statement 3 is incorrect: Unni Krishnan held free education until age 14 flows from Article 21, and there is no such right to a professional degree. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct.

passages.title: India's BRICS Chairship 2026
passages.text:
India formally took over the BRICS chairship from Brazil on 1 January 2026, becoming chair of the grouping for the fourth time. Twelve days later, on 13 January, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar unveiled the logo, website and theme of the presidency in New Delhi. The theme, "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability", was tied by officials to the people-centric approach Prime Minister Narendra Modi had outlined at the previous year's summit in Rio de Janeiro. The chairship runs for the calendar year, from 1 January to 31 December, and the chair sets the agenda for meetings at every level, from sherpas and ministers to the leaders' summit.

The calendar of ministerial meetings began to fill in the middle of the year. Foreign ministers and heads of delegation from member and partner countries gathered at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on 14 and 15 May 2026. Jaishankar chaired the meeting, which was overshadowed by the crisis in West Asia, and the delegates later called on Modi. On 22 and 23 June, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval hosted the 16th meeting of BRICS national security advisers in the capital. Russia's Security Council Secretary Sergey Shoigu and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi were among those who attended. The agenda was built around non-traditional security challenges, and Doval used the sidelines to hold bilateral talks with officials from Iran, Brazil, Ethiopia and South Africa.

The presidency culminated in the 18th BRICS Summit, held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, on 12 and 13 September 2026. On the first day, Modi announced that leaders had adopted the New Delhi Declaration by consensus, with no member raising an objection. Reports said hard negotiations, which ran until the early hours, were needed to bridge sharp differences between Iran and the United Arab Emirates over the West Asia conflict, with India acting as mediator. The 140-paragraph document ranges across global governance reform, peace and security, trade and finance, technology, climate and people-to-people cooperation. It backed a larger role for India and Brazil at the United Nations, criticised unilateral tariffs and secondary sanctions, and condemned the 22 April 2025 terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir. It also called for a ceasefire in Gaza and endorsed India-led initiatives on financial risk, artificial intelligence and big-cat conservation.

The declaration also welcomed what it called significant progress under India's presidency and pledged support for China, which will take over the rotating chair in 2027. India's turn came at a time when the bloc, which has expanded considerably through enlargement in recent years, is trying to balance members with very different positions on the conflicts in West Asia. Reports described the ability to produce a consensus text, even after hard bargaining, as a major diplomatic win for India at the Delhi summit.

questions.q: The BRICS grouping's own multilateral lender, the New Development Bank, has its headquarters in which city?
questions.explanation: Article 3 of the Agreement on the New Development Bank (signed at Fortaleza, 15 July 2014) places the Bank's headquarters in Shanghai; its first regional office is in Johannesburg.

questions.q: Which BRICS member held the rotating chair in 2024, the year before Brazil?
questions.explanation: Russia chaired BRICS in 2024 (the Kazan summit, 22-24 October 2024), followed by Brazil in 2025 and India in 2026.

questions.assertion: Indonesia is a full member of BRICS.
questions.reason: Brazil held the rotating BRICS chair in 2025.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true: Indonesia was announced as a full member on 6 January 2025, and Brazil chaired BRICS in 2025. Brazil's holding the chair does not explain why Indonesia is a member (its entry was approved by consensus of the members), so R does not explain A.
Sanya, China hosted the 2011 summit (South Africa's first as a full member); New Delhi hosted in 2012; Durban in 2013; Fortaleza in 2014, where the New Development Bank agreement was signed.

statements: I. India's most recent chairship of BRICS before 2026 was in 2021.
II. South Africa's admission in 2010 led the BRIC grouping to be renamed BRICS.
questions.explanation: India's earlier chairships were 2012, 2016 and 2021, so 2021 was its most recent before 2026. South Africa was invited to join in December 2010, and BRIC became BRICS.

statements: 1. The acronym BRIC was coined in 2001 by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill.
2. The first formal BRIC leaders' summit was held in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in June 2009.
3. South Africa's first summit as a full member of the grouping was held in 2011.
4. The Agreement on the New Development Bank was signed in 2013.
questions.explanation: Statement 4 is incorrect: the 2013 Durban summit agreed to set up the bank, and the agreement was signed at Fortaleza on 15 July 2014. Statements 1-3 are correct.

passages.title: PSLV-C62 failure and the road to Gaganyaan
passages.text:
The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) began 2026 with a setback. On 12 January 2026, its Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle mission PSLV-C62 lifted off from Sriharikota carrying EOS-N1, a strategic hyperspectral Earth-observation satellite also referred to as Anvesha, along with 15 co-passenger payloads belonging to Indian and foreign organisations. The first two stages performed as planned, but ISRO reported an anomaly at the end of the third stage, known as PS3. ISRO chairman V. Narayanan said a disturbance in the rocket's roll rate had pushed the vehicle off its flight path, and the payloads did not reach their intended orbit. Among the lost payloads were Theos-2, an Earth-observation satellite built jointly by the United Kingdom and Thailand, and AyulSat, a refuelling demonstrator. The Spanish prototype Kestrel Initial Demonstrator was reported to have transmitted some data.

The failure drew attention because it was the second consecutive loss for the workhorse rocket. The previous mission, PSLV-C61 in May 2025, had also failed owing to a problem in the third stage. After C62, ISRO announced a failure analysis committee. News reports citing sources said a probe had been set up under K. VijayRaghavan, a former Principal Scientific Advisor to the Prime Minister, with former ISRO chairman S. Somanath as co-chairman.

The episode has implications for India's human spaceflight plans. The Gaganyaan programme, which aims to send Indian astronauts to low Earth orbit, depends on a series of uncrewed test flights. In October 2025 Narayanan said the first of these, G1, which will carry the half-humanoid robot Vyommitra, was about 90 per cent complete and planned for December. In June 2026 he said ISRO was aiming to launch it by the end of 2026, though it could slip into 2027. The mission will use a human-rated launch vehicle. ISRO has said that three uncrewed missions will precede it.

Meanwhile, India is also building new launch infrastructure. A second spaceport, intended mainly for small satellite launches, has been under construction since March 2025, with commissioning provisionally targeted for the financial year 2026-27.

questions.q: The Sriharikota spaceport, from which PSLV-C62 was launched, is officially named after which scientist and former ISRO chairman?
questions.explanation: Sriharikota (earlier SHAR) hosts the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, renamed in 2002 in memory of Prof. Satish Dhawan, former ISRO chairman.

questions.assertion: India's planned second spaceport at Kulasekarapattinam is intended mainly for launching small satellites on the SSLV.
questions.reason: A launch site on the southern tip of the peninsula lets rockets fly directly south to polar orbits, avoiding the curved trajectory that Sriharikota launches need to stay clear of Sri Lanka.
questions.explanation: Kulasekarapattinam is planned for SSLV launches to Sun-synchronous polar orbits; its southern location allows a straight southward path, whereas launches from Sriharikota have to curve to avoid Sri Lanka.

list1: II. Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (lead centre for launch vehicles)
questions.explanation: ISRO is headquartered in Bengaluru; VSSC is in Thiruvananthapuram; Sriharikota island lies in Tirupati district of Andhra Pradesh; Kulasekarapattinam is in Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu.

statements: I. The PSLV is a four-stage vehicle whose third stage (PS3) uses solid propellant.
II. The very first PSLV flight, PSLV-D1 on 20 September 1993, successfully placed its satellite in orbit.
questions.explanation: PSLV alternates solid-liquid-solid-liquid, so PS3 is solid (HTPB-based). PSLV-D1 in 1993 failed because of an attitude-control problem at stage separation, so the satellite was not placed in orbit.

statements: I. ISRO was formed on 15 August 1969, succeeding the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) set up in 1962.
II. ISRO's headquarters is located in Thiruvananthapuram.
III. ISRO functions under the Department of Space.
questions.explanation: ISRO succeeded INCOSPAR on 15 August 1969 and is managed by the Department of Space; its headquarters is in Bengaluru, not Thiruvananthapuram (where VSSC is).

questions.q: The uncrewed Gaganyaan test flight G1 is planned on a human-rated version of which ISRO launch vehicle?
questions.explanation: Gaganyaan uses HLVM3, the human-rated variant of the LVM3 (formerly GSLV Mk III), launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre.
